narration.text:
听一段小故事：米娅找到钥匙。她打开了门。第二句不必再说一遍“米娅”，因为“她”会把我们带回刚出现的人。英语也是这样：<#0.4#>Mia found the key. She opened the door。<#0.8#>She 没有介绍新人，而是指回 Mia，再接着说她的新动作。这个从 Mia 到 She 的联系叫指代链。要是前文同时出现 Mia 和 Lucy，突然来一句 She opened the door，读者就可能不知道“她”是谁。
句子能连起来，不只靠人称代词。<#0.4#>The experiment failed. This result surprised us。<#0.7#>这里 This result 指的不是 experiment 这个东西，而是“实验失败”这件事。它先把前一句打包接住，再让后一句对这件事作评价。重复关键词、用替代词、省略已知内容，也都能帮助读者沿着同一条线往下读。这些看得见的连接线索，叫衔接。
但有连接词，不代表意思一定通。The sky was clear. Therefore, I forgot my keys 里，therefore 声称前后是因果，可“天晴”并不会自然导致“忘带钥匙”。形式接上了，逻辑没有接上，文章仍然不连贯。<#0.8#>
检查时做三件事：看到 he、she、it、this 先问它能不能唯一指回某个对象或事件；看到 therefore、however 等词，核对前后逻辑是否真实；最后看每句有没有接住已知信息，再推进一个与主题有关的新信息。

course.title: Reference chains with personal pronouns
course.meta: Tracking the same participant across sentences
examples: Mia bought a camera. She uses it every day.
The students entered. They sat down.
The bus was late. It caused a long wait.

analyses.label: Subject; refers to the preceding situation

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: She returns to Mia and it to camera; each pronoun continues an established referent.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: students denotes several people, and They keeps that plural reference chain stable.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: caused a long wait evaluates the late-bus situation, so It summarizes the preceding event.

rules: A personal pronoun normally refers back to an established person or thing, avoiding full repetition.
Pronouns in one reference chain should maintain stable person, number and referent.
it can refer to a thing or to a previously mentioned event or situation; the following predicate helps identify it.

questions.question: Who does She refer back to?
questions.correct: Person and meaning match Mia.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Person and meaning match Mia.

questions.question: Why is They used?

options.text: It treats students as one inanimate unit

questions.correct: The pronoun agrees in number with its antecedent.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The pronoun agrees in number with its antecedent.

questions.question: What does It most naturally refer to?

options.text: The fact that the bus was late

questions.correct: caused a long wait applies to the whole situation.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: caused a long wait applies to the whole situation.

course.title: Possessive forms across sentences
course.meta: Referring to an owner while determining a following noun
examples: Leo joined the club. His coach welcomed him.
My answer is short. Yours is detailed.
Tom told Jack that his plan had failed.

analyses.label: Clause linker + subject; his has two candidates

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: His both refers back to Leo and determines coach, yielding Leo’s coach.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Yours fills the subject slot in the new sentence and expands to your answer.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Both Tom and Jack match his, so formal agreement does not identify the owner.

rules: A possessive determiner refers back to an owner and determines a following noun in the new sentence.
An independent possessive pronoun substitutes for possessive determiner + noun, whose noun must be recoverable.
When two possible owners are present, his/her/their may be ambiguous; repeat a noun or name.

questions.question: Who does His refer to?
questions.correct: Leo is the owner.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Leo is the owner.

questions.question: What does Yours substitute for?
questions.correct: The contrast is between two answers.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The contrast is between two answers.

questions.question: What is the problem with his plan?

options.text: It is unclear whether the plan is Tom’s or Jack’s
The nearest noun uniquely fixes Jack as owner

questions.correct: Both masculine singular candidates match his.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Both masculine singular candidates match his.

course.title: Forward reference and later identification
course.meta: Using a pronoun before its identifying expression
examples: Before he spoke, Mr Li checked his notes.
When she entered, the new principal smiled.
The new policy was announced today. It starts next month.

analyses.label: Subject; refers to the new policy

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: he appears first and Mr Li immediately supplies the identity; this is forward reference resolved later.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The identity of she follows immediately in the same sentence, so the reader waits only briefly.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The new policy is established before It continues it, reducing tracking effort in exposition.

rules: Pronouns usually refer backward, but some styles allow them to refer forward to a later noun phrase.
A forward reference must be resolved quickly by a clear identifying expression, or readers lose orientation.
Formal exposition normally introduces the noun first and then uses a pronoun, avoiding unnecessary forward-reference load.

questions.question: Who does he refer forward to?
questions.correct: The following main-clause subject identifies the referent.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The following main-clause subject identifies the referent.

questions.question: Why is this forward reference understandable?

options.text: The identity appears only in the next paragraph

questions.correct: The identifying phrase is immediate and clear.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The identifying phrase is immediate and clear.

questions.question: Which order better suits exposition?
questions.correct: The entity is established before pronoun continuation.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The entity is established before pronoun continuation.

course.title: Antecedent agreement
course.meta: Matching number, person, meaning and reference range
examples: The committee members arrived. They took their seats.
Someone left a bag. They may return for it.
The laptop was beside the printer. It needed more ink.

analyses.label: Subject; singular they referring to someone

analyses.text: The laptop was beside the printer.
analyses.label: Clause/sentence information

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The actual antecedent head is plural members, so They is required despite nearby committee.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: They and someone refer to one person of unknown gender, the standard singular they.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Both nouns match it formally, but ink makes printer the sensible referent.

rules: A pronoun must agree in number with its antecedent.
With an indefinite antecedent, modern English often uses singular they for gender-neutral reference.
Formal agreement is not enough; the pronoun must also make semantic sense with its candidate antecedent.

questions.question: Why is They used?

options.text: It refers to plural head members
It treats committee as one unit

questions.correct: The actual antecedent head is plural members.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The actual antecedent head is plural members.

questions.question: Does They necessarily mean several people here?

options.text: No; it refers to singular someone

questions.correct: Singular they can refer to a person of unknown gender.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Singular they can refer to a person of unknown gender.

questions.question: What does It most reasonably refer to?
questions.correct: A printer normally needs ink.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: A printer normally needs ink.

course.title: Clarity and ambiguity
course.meta: A pronoun should have one reasonable candidate
examples: Anna called Lily. She sounded worried.
Anna called Lily. Lily sounded worried.
They say the rule will change.

analyses.label: Subject; two candidates, Anna and Lily

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: She has two equally plausible female candidates, Anna and Lily, so the reader cannot choose uniquely.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Repeating Lily sacrifices a little brevity but produces one stable interpretation.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: They has no identifiable source; formal writing should name who makes the claim.

rules: A pronoun is easily ambiguous when several nearby candidates match in gender and number.
The most reliable disambiguation is to repeat a name or role rather than forcing readers to guess the nearest noun.
Avoid vague this, it or they: if readers cannot replace it with a clear noun phrase, the reference may be unclear.

questions.question: What is wrong with She?

options.text: It may refer to Anna or Lily

questions.correct: Both candidates match she.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Both candidates match she.

questions.question: Whom does the revision identify as worried?
questions.correct: Repeating Lily removes ambiguity.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Repeating Lily removes ambiguity.

questions.question: How can formal exposition improve it?

options.text: Keep they to leave the source broad

questions.correct: Source they has no identifiable antecedent.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Source they has no identifiable antecedent.

course.title: Reference distance and multiple candidates
course.meta: Greater distance and more candidates require fuller naming
examples: The survey began in May. Several teams collected data through summer. After three revisions, the survey was published.
The doctor spoke to the patient after the nurse arrived. She then explained the result.
The doctor spoke to the patient. The nurse then explained the result.

analyses.text: The survey began in May. Several teams collected data through summer.
analyses.label: Prior context
Subject; repeats a distant topic noun

analyses.text: The doctor spoke to the patient after the nurse arrived.
analyses.label: Clause/sentence information

analyses.text: The doctor spoke to the patient.
analyses.label: Clause/sentence information

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: After several intervening nouns, repeating the survey reactivates the distant topic.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: She may denote doctor or nurse; nearest-noun guessing cannot replace semantic and discourse reasoning.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The revision names The nurse, leaving only one performer for the second action.

rules: When a pronoun is far from its antecedent, working-memory load increases; repeat a name or noun phrase.
The nearest noun is not an absolute rule; combine agreement, semantic role and discourse topic.
With multiple candidates, reorder, repeat role names or split sentences so each pronoun has one plausible antecedent.

questions.question: Why repeat the survey in the last clause?

options.text: The antecedent is distant with intervening nouns
The nearest noun teams is the item published

questions.correct: Repeating the noun reactivates the topic.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Repeating the noun reactivates the topic.

questions.question: Is She uniquely resolved?

options.text: Yes; it must mean nearest nurse
No; doctor and nurse may both fit

questions.correct: Context or a repeated role noun is needed.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Context or a repeated role noun is needed.

questions.question: What does the revision remove?
questions.correct: It explicitly assigns the second action to the nurse.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: It explicitly assigns the second action to the nurse.

course.title: Discourse this and that
course.meta: Turning a previous proposition into the next sentence’s topic
examples: The school extended library hours. This helped students study.
The school extended library hours. This decision helped students study.
He rejected every suggestion. That attitude frustrated the team.

analyses.label: Subject; refers to the preceding action
Subject; summarizes the preceding sentence as a decision

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: This refers to the whole extension of hours and places that action in the subject slot of helped.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: decision classifies bare this, telling the reader to interpret the previous sentence as a decision.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: That attitude both refers back to the rejection and evaluates it as an attitude.

rules: this and that can refer to the whole preceding proposition, not only the nearest noun.
Bare this may be vague; this + summary noun states how the previous information is interpreted.
that often suggests greater distance, completion or evaluative detachment, though context controls the contrast.

questions.question: What does This refer to?
questions.correct: helped students study evaluates the whole action.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: helped students study evaluates the whole action.

questions.question: What does decision do?

options.text: It labels the previous sentence as a decision

questions.correct: The summary noun creates a clear discourse relation.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The summary noun creates a clear discourse relation.

questions.question: How does That attitude summarize the previous sentence?

options.text: It evaluates rejecting suggestions as an attitude
It refers only to the noun suggestion

questions.correct: that + attitude evaluates the preceding behaviour.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: that + attitude evaluates the preceding behaviour.

course.title: Discourse these and those
course.meta: Referring to sets and building classification contrasts
examples: The plan needs time, money, and staff. These are difficult to secure.
Online classes offer flexibility and save travel time. These benefits matter to working students.
The server failed twice. These incidents delayed the launch.

analyses.text: The plan needs time, money, and staff.
analyses.label: Three requirements

analyses.text: Online classes offer flexibility and save travel time.
analyses.label: Two preceding advantages

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: These groups time, money and staff as a plural set for one following evaluation.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: These benefits classifies both flexibility and saved travel time as advantages, then evaluates their importance to working students together.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The previous sentence contains two failures, and These incidents summarizes both events in the plural.

rules: these can refer back to a newly listed set and continue discussing it as a group.
these/those + summary noun can group several preceding items and continue evaluating the set.
The number of these/those must match the summarized items; a single event normally takes this/that.

questions.question: What does These refer to?
questions.correct: The plural demonstrative summarizes the three items.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The plural demonstrative summarizes the three items.

questions.question: What does These benefits summarize?

options.text: online classes and students as two groups

questions.correct: The plural summary noun groups the two advantages.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The plural summary noun groups the two advantages.

questions.question: Why use These incidents?

options.text: It treats server as several machines

questions.correct: The antecedent information contains multiple events.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The antecedent information contains multiple events.

course.title: Nominal substitution with one/ones
course.meta: Keeping the class while replacing a repeated count noun
examples: I need a pen. Do you have a blue one?
These shoes are heavy. I prefer the light ones.
This coffee is bitter. I would like some from that pot.

analyses.label: Subject; starting point of the later sentence
Subject; starting point of the later sentence

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: blue one keeps the contrastive information blue and replaces the known class noun pen.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: light ones corresponds to plural shoes while retaining number and the contrast light.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: coffee is an uncountable substance here, so some refers to an amount rather than one to a count item.

rules: one substitutes for a preceding singular count noun, avoiding repetition while preserving class meaning.
ones substitutes for plural count nouns and normally carries a determiner or modifier.
one/ones cannot mechanically replace an uncountable noun; repeat it, use some or revise.

questions.question: What does one substitute for?
questions.correct: blue one means blue pen.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: blue one means blue pen.

questions.question: Why is ones plural?

options.text: It refers to one singular shoe

questions.correct: The substitute matches the noun in number.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The substitute matches the noun in number.

questions.question: Why is some used rather than one here?

options.text: coffee is treated as an uncountable substance
coffee is counted as one serving here

questions.correct: one substitutes for a singular count noun.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: one substitutes for a singular count noun.

course.title: Verbal substitution with do
course.meta: Retaining an operator instead of repeating an action
examples: Mia studies harder than Tom does.
Can Mia swim? Yes, she can.
Mia likes tea, and her friends do too.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: does has Tom as its new subject and recovers only Tom studies; the degree is supplied by the harder than comparison, so Tom studies hard must not be added.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The short answer retains only operator can; she and the question recover the full range can swim, not merely the word swim.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: do recovers the full preceding predicate likes tea, while its form agrees with new plural subject her friends.

rules: do/does/did can substitute for a preceding simple-tense lexical predicate, while comparative degree remains supplied by the comparison.
An auxiliary or modal can itself substitute for the rest of a predicate in a short response.
The substitute must fit the new subject, tense and modality rather than mechanically copying form.

questions.question: What range does does recover?
questions.correct: does recovers only Tom studies; harder than expresses the degree.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: does recovers only Tom studies; harder than expresses the degree.

questions.question: What full range does can recover?
questions.correct: The operator and context recover can swim.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The operator and context recover can swim.

questions.question: Why is do used instead of does?

options.text: It still agrees with singular Mia in the first clause

questions.correct: The substitute operator agrees with the new subject.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The substitute operator agrees with the new subject.

course.title: Clausal substitution with so and not
course.meta: Replacing a whole proposition instead of repeating a that-clause
examples: Will it rain? I think so.
Will the flight be delayed? I hope not.
The price may rise and delivery may slow. I think so.

analyses.label: Subject; so substitutes for a positive proposition
Subject; not substitutes for a negative proposition

analyses.text: The price may rise and delivery may slow.
analyses.label: Two candidate propositions
Subject; so has multiple candidate propositions

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: so does not refer to the word rain; it replaces the full proposition that it will rain.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: hope not places the negation in not and avoids repeating the flight will not be delayed.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The previous sentence contains two propositions, price rising and delivery slowing, so I think so cannot show which one—or whether both—is intended.

rules: After think, hope, believe and suppose, so can replace a preceding positive proposition.
not can replace a negative proposition in selected patterns with hope, think and similar verbs, but the construction is verb-sensitive.
The proposition replaced by so/not must be clear; if several candidates exist, repeat the key content.

questions.question: What does so substitute for?
questions.correct: so substitutes for the whole proposition.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: so substitutes for the whole proposition.

questions.question: What does not substitute for?

options.text: the flight will not be delayed

questions.correct: I hope not means I hope the flight will not be delayed.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: I hope not means I hope the flight will not be delayed.

questions.question: What is the problem with so?

options.text: It is unclear whether it means price, delivery or both

questions.correct: The previous sentence offers multiple propositions.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The previous sentence offers multiple propositions.

course.title: The boundary between ellipsis and substitution
course.meta: Substitution leaves a form; ellipsis leaves a recoverable gap
examples: I chose the red pen, and Mia chose the blue one.
I chose the red pen; Mia, the blue.
Tom likes Mia more than Jack.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: In blue one, one is an overt substitute for pen; this is not zero ellipsis.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Mia, the blue omits both predicate chose and noun pen; parallelism with the first clause recovers Mia chose the blue pen.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: than Jack can recover as than Tom likes Jack or than Jack likes Mia; two valid recoveries produce different meanings.

rules: Substitution uses an overt form such as one, do or so in place of preceding material.
Ellipsis leaves no substitute; missing material is recovered from parallel structure.
Use ellipsis only when recovery is clear and unique; otherwise use substitution or repeat key wording.

questions.question: What cohesive device is one?
questions.correct: An overt substitute one remains.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: An overt substitute one remains.

questions.question: What is the full recovery of the second clause?
questions.correct: Parallelism recovers both predicate chose and noun pen.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Parallelism recovers both predicate chose and noun pen.

questions.question: Why can this be ambiguous?

options.text: It can only recover as Jack likes Mia
It may recover likes Jack or Jack likes Mia

questions.correct: Two recoveries fit the surface structure.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Two recoveries fit the surface structure.

course.title: Keyword repetition as a topic chain
course.meta: Strategic repetition can be clearer than constant variation
examples: Solar energy is becoming cheaper. Solar energy also reduces emissions.
The team measured anxiety on Monday. The anxiety measurement was repeated weekly.
The new app saves time. It also reduces errors.

analyses.label: Later subject referring to the measurement event
Subject; refers to the new app

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Both sentences repeat Solar energy in topic position, then add separate information about cost and emissions.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The anxiety measurement repeats anxiety and accurately refers to the preceding measurement event without introducing the meaning of a scale.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The new app establishes the referent and It then tracks it, keeping the topic while avoiding mechanical full-noun repetition.

rules: A paragraph’s key term should be repeated strategically to keep the topic stable.
Randomly replacing a technical term with near-synonyms may shift its meaning; accuracy takes priority over avoiding repetition.
Mechanical repetition of a full noun in every sentence is heavy; once clear, use pronouns, summary nouns or ellipsis.

questions.question: What does repeating Solar energy do?
questions.correct: Readers can immediately track the paragraph subject.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Readers can immediately track the paragraph subject.

questions.question: Why retain anxiety?

options.text: To use any near-synonym to avoid repetition
To preserve the same measured construct

questions.correct: Keyword repetition preserves conceptual identity.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Keyword repetition preserves conceptual identity.

questions.question: How does It improve cohesion?

options.text: It avoids repetition while retaining app reference

questions.correct: The antecedent is unique and nearby, so the pronoun is clear.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The antecedent is unique and nearby, so the pronoun is clear.

course.title: Cohesion through lexical relations
course.meta: Varying wording within a semantic field without changing the concept
examples: The task was difficult. This hard task took two hours.
Roses, tulips, and lilies filled the garden. These flowers attracted bees.
The report describes a delay. This disaster affected two meetings.

analyses.label: Subject; near-synonymous reference to the same task

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: hard and difficult both describe task difficulty here; hard task refers to the same task without adding a category such as assignment.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Roses, tulips and lilies are hyponyms, and flowers is the superordinate that groups them.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: delay and disaster are not neutral alternatives; disaster adds strong negative evaluation and exaggerates the delay.

rules: Synonymous or near-synonymous wording can reduce monotony, but meaning must remain stable and no new category should be smuggled in.
A superordinate can summarize specific items, while hyponyms can develop a general topic.
A lexical replacement that changes evaluation or scope causes conceptual drift; return to the accurate key term.

questions.question: How does hard task link to the first sentence?

options.text: assignment adds a category to task
hard echoes difficult while task stays stable

questions.correct: The synonymous adjective does not change the task category.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The synonymous adjective does not change the task category.

questions.question: What is the relation between flowers and the first three items?
questions.correct: flowers summarizes the three kinds.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: flowers summarizes the three kinds.

questions.question: What is problematic about disaster?

options.text: It exaggerates delay into a disaster

questions.correct: The replacement changes evaluative force.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The replacement changes evaluative force.

course.title: Basic logical connections
course.meta: and, but and so mark addition, contrast and result
examples: The method is simple, and it is inexpensive.
The method is simple, but it is slow.
The road was closed, so we changed routes.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: and adds inexpensive to simple, and both support a positive evaluation.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: but makes slow qualify the positive expectation created by simple.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: so marks changed routes as the result of the road being closed.

rules: and links additive information or sequential progression.
but marks contrast, qualification or counter-expectation between clauses.
so marks the second clause as a result of the first.

questions.question: What does and express?
questions.correct: The second point supports the same direction.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The second point supports the same direction.

questions.question: How does the but-clause relate to the first?
questions.correct: slow qualifies the positive evaluation of simple.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: slow qualifies the positive evaluation of simple.

questions.question: Which is the result?
questions.correct: The closure causes the route change.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The closure causes the route change.

course.title: Conjunctive adverbs and punctuation
course.meta: however and therefore signal logic while punctuation carries the clause boundary
examples: The plan was costly; however, it was effective.
The data were incomplete; therefore, we repeated the test.
The plan, however, remained unchanged.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: however signals contrast, while the semicolon carries the boundary between independent clauses.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The semicolon closes the first independent clause, and the comma then sets off therefore.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: however can move inside the clause; commas show that it is outside the core clause structure.

rules: however marks contrast and therefore marks result; they are conjunctive adverbs, not coordinators.
When a conjunctive adverb links independent clauses, use a semicolon or full stop before it and normally a comma after it.
A conjunctive adverb can move within the clause, but its logical link must remain clear and punctuation must set it off appropriately.

questions.question: What does however express?
questions.correct: Effectiveness contrasts with cost.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Effectiveness contrasts with cost.

questions.question: Which punctuation is standard?
questions.correct: The semicolon establishes the clause boundary; the comma sets off the connector.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The semicolon establishes the clause boundary; the comma sets off the connector.

questions.question: What is however within the clause?
questions.correct: Commas mark the parenthetical position.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Commas mark the parenthetical position.

course.title: Time and sequence connections
course.meta: first, then, meanwhile and finally organize a process
examples: First, collect the data. Then, check each entry.
The team analysed the results. Meanwhile, the manager prepared the report.
Several attempts failed. Eventually, the team found a solution.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: First and Then place collection and checking in their real procedural order.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Meanwhile marks the two activities as parallel, not causal.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Eventually depends on the preceding failed attempts, making the solution the process endpoint.

rules: first, next, then and finally mark procedural order and must match the real sequence.
meanwhile marks processes occurring in parallel during the same period.
eventually/finally marks an endpoint in a process; do not use it merely because a sentence is last.

questions.question: What does Then mark?
questions.correct: It places checking after collection.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: It places checking after collection.

questions.question: What relation does Meanwhile express?
questions.correct: The two activities unfold in the same period.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The two activities unfold in the same period.

questions.question: Why is Eventually appropriate?

options.text: A sequence of attempts precedes it

questions.correct: Finding the solution is the endpoint.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Finding the solution is the endpoint.

course.title: Example, restatement and summary connections
course.meta: for example, in other words and overall signal discourse functions
examples: Many habits save energy. For example, turning off lights reduces waste.
The rule is optional. In other words, you may choose whether to use it.
The device is cheap, reliable, and easy to use. Overall, it is a practical choice.

analyses.text: The device is cheap, reliable, and easy to use.
analyses.label: Clause/sentence information

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The first sentence gives a general claim, and For example supplies turning off lights as one instance.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: In other words preserves the proposition and explains optional more plainly.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Overall synthesizes cheap, reliable and easy into practical rather than repeating one detail.

rules: for example and for instance introduce a specific instance of a general claim.
in other words and that is restate or clarify previous content and should not introduce a contradictory new point.
overall, in summary and to sum up synthesize the main conclusion rather than repeat one detail.

lessons.title: Definition, core and scope of cohesion and reference
lessons.meta: Helping readers track referents, read relations and follow topic development across sentences
examples: Mia found the key. She opened the door.

The sky was clear. Therefore, I forgot my keys.

analyses.label: Subject; starting point of the later sentence

exampleNotes.body: She does not introduce a new person; it takes the reader back to Mia, so both sentences continue the same participant.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: This result packages the whole failed experiment as the next subject; it links meanings across sentences rather than merely referring to the noun experiment.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Therefore is an explicit cohesive marker, but it cannot make clear skies logically cause forgotten keys; cohesive form does not guarantee coherence.

rules: Cohesion is not word-class labelling inside one sentence; it uses identifiable expressions to connect a later sentence to an earlier referent.
Reference may connect people, things or whole events; substitution and ellipsis avoid repeated structure, but each must be accurately recoverable from context.
Cohesion is visible linguistic linkage, while coherence is meaningful unity; an explicit connector cannot repair faulty logic, and a coherent context may omit connectors.

narration.text:
听一段小故事：米娅找到钥匙。她打开了门。第二句不必再说一遍“米娅”，因为“她”会把我们带回刚出现的人。英语也是这样：<#0.4#>Mia found the key. She opened the door。<#0.8#>She 没有介绍新人，而是指回 Mia，再接着说她的新动作。这个从 Mia 到 She 的联系叫指代链。要是前文同时出现 Mia 和 Lucy，突然来一句 She opened the door，读者就可能不知道“她”是谁。
句子能连起来，不只靠人称代词。<#0.4#>The experiment failed. This result surprised us。<#0.7#>这里 This result 指的不是 experiment 这个东西，而是“实验失败”这件事。它先把前一句打包接住，再让后一句对这件事作评价。重复关键词、用替代词、省略已知内容，也都能帮助读者沿着同一条线往下读。这些看得见的连接线索，叫衔接。
但有连接词，不代表意思一定通。The sky was clear. Therefore, I forgot my keys 里，therefore 声称前后是因果，可“天晴”并不会自然导致“忘带钥匙”。形式接上了，逻辑没有接上，文章仍然不连贯。<#0.8#>
检查时做三件事：看到 he、she、it、this 先问它能不能唯一指回某个对象或事件；看到 therefore、however 等词，核对前后逻辑是否真实；最后看每句有没有接住已知信息，再推进一个与主题有关的新信息。

lessons.title: Basic logical connections
lessons.meta: and, but and so mark addition, contrast and result
examples: The method is simple, and it is inexpensive.
The method is simple, but it is slow.
The road was closed, so we changed routes.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: and adds inexpensive to simple, and both support a positive evaluation.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: but makes slow qualify the positive expectation created by simple.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: so marks changed routes as the result of the road being closed.

rules: and links additive information or sequential progression.
but marks contrast, qualification or counter-expectation between clauses.
so marks the second clause as a result of the first.

questions.correct: The second point supports the same direction.

questions.question: How does the but-clause relate to the first?
questions.correct: slow qualifies the positive evaluation of simple.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: slow qualifies the positive evaluation of simple.

questions.question: Which is the result?
questions.correct: The closure causes the route change.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The closure causes the route change.

lessons.title: Conjunctive adverbs and punctuation
lessons.meta: however and therefore signal logic while punctuation carries the clause boundary
examples: The plan was costly; however, it was effective.
The data were incomplete; therefore, we repeated the test.
The plan, however, remained unchanged.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: however signals contrast, while the semicolon carries the boundary between independent clauses.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The semicolon closes the first independent clause, and the comma then sets off therefore.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: however can move inside the clause; commas show that it is outside the core clause structure.

rules: however marks contrast and therefore marks result; they are conjunctive adverbs, not coordinators.
When a conjunctive adverb links independent clauses, use a semicolon or full stop before it and normally a comma after it.
A conjunctive adverb can move within the clause, but its logical link must remain clear and punctuation must set it off appropriately.

questions.question: What does however express?
questions.correct: Effectiveness contrasts with cost.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Effectiveness contrasts with cost.

questions.question: Which punctuation is standard?
questions.correct: The semicolon establishes the clause boundary; the comma sets off the connector.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The semicolon establishes the clause boundary; the comma sets off the connector.

questions.question: What is however within the clause?
questions.correct: Commas mark the parenthetical position.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Commas mark the parenthetical position.

lessons.title: Time and sequence connections
lessons.meta: first, then, meanwhile and finally organize a process
examples: First, collect the data. Then, check each entry.
The team analysed the results. Meanwhile, the manager prepared the report.
Several attempts failed. Eventually, the team found a solution.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: First and Then place collection and checking in their real procedural order.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Meanwhile marks the two activities as parallel, not causal.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Eventually depends on the preceding failed attempts, making the solution the process endpoint.

rules: first, next, then and finally mark procedural order and must match the real sequence.
meanwhile marks processes occurring in parallel during the same period.
eventually/finally marks an endpoint in a process; do not use it merely because a sentence is last.

questions.question: What does Then mark?
questions.correct: It places checking after collection.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: It places checking after collection.

questions.question: What relation does Meanwhile express?
questions.correct: The two activities unfold in the same period.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The two activities unfold in the same period.

questions.question: Why is Eventually appropriate?

options.text: A sequence of attempts precedes it

questions.correct: Finding the solution is the endpoint.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Finding the solution is the endpoint.

lessons.title: Example, restatement and summary connections
lessons.meta: for example, in other words and overall signal discourse functions
examples: Many habits save energy. For example, turning off lights reduces waste.
The rule is optional. In other words, you may choose whether to use it.
The device is cheap, reliable, and easy to use. Overall, it is a practical choice.

analyses.text: The device is cheap, reliable, and easy to use.
analyses.label: Clause/sentence information

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The first sentence gives a general claim, and For example supplies turning off lights as one instance.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: In other words preserves the proposition and explains optional more plainly.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Overall synthesizes cheap, reliable and easy into practical rather than repeating one detail.

rules: for example and for instance introduce a specific instance of a general claim.
in other words and that is restate or clarify previous content and should not introduce a contradictory new point.
overall, in summary and to sum up synthesize the main conclusion rather than repeat one detail.

questions.question: How does the second sentence relate to the first?
questions.correct: Turning off lights exemplifies an energy-saving habit.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Turning off lights exemplifies an energy-saving habit.

questions.question: What does In other words signal?
questions.correct: The second sentence explains optional.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The second sentence explains optional.

questions.question: What does the Overall-sentence do?
questions.correct: practical choice is the overall evaluation.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: practical choice is the overall evaluation.

lessons.title: Articles and given-new information
lessons.meta: a/an introduces; the tracks an established entity
examples: I saw a dog outside.
The dog was wet. It looked cold.
Please close the door near the stairs.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: a dog introduces a countable referent that the reader was not expected to identify beforehand.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: the dog and It both track the established dog, attaching new information to a given referent.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: near the stairs supplies enough restriction for the listener to identify the door in context.

rules: a/an commonly introduces a singular count entity as new discourse information.
On subsequent mention, the or a pronoun commonly marks the same entity as given information.
the can establish identifiability through shared knowledge, uniqueness or following specification, not only prior mention.

questions.question: What does a dog signal?
questions.correct: The indefinite article establishes a new referent.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The indefinite article establishes a new referent.

questions.question: Why is The dog used?

options.text: It introduces a dog not mentioned before
The entity has already been introduced

questions.correct: The definite article tracks the established referent.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The definite article tracks the established referent.

questions.question: Why is the used?

options.text: near the stairs identifies the door
The speaker introduces any door for the first time

questions.correct: The postmodifier narrows the reference to a specific entity.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The postmodifier narrows the reference to a specific entity.

lessons.title: Paragraph topic chains
lessons.meta: Balancing topic continuity and progression
examples: Urban trees reduce heat. They also improve air quality.
Urban trees reduce heat. They also absorb rainwater.
Urban trees need maintenance. City budgets, however, are often limited.

analyses.label: Subject; continues the topic and adds new information

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: Urban trees establishes the topic, They continues it, and improve air quality adds new information.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The second sentence keeps the topic but advances the comment from cooling to rainwater absorption.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: City budgets explicitly names a new topic, while however marks its limiting relation to maintenance needs.

rules: A paragraph establishes a central topic, and later sentences maintain it through repetition, pronouns or summary nouns.
Each sentence should add new information to the established topic rather than merely paraphrase without progress.
When the topic shifts abruptly, use an explicit noun and transition rather than a vague pronoun.

questions.question: What is the discourse role of They?

options.text: It continues the urban trees topic

questions.correct: The pronoun maintains the same topic chain.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The pronoun maintains the same topic chain.

questions.question: How does the second sentence progress?
questions.correct: The topic remains while the comment adds information.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The topic remains while the comment adds information.

questions.question: Why name City budgets rather than use They?

options.text: To continue referring to urban trees
The paragraph shifts to a new topic

questions.correct: The explicit noun prevents reference back to trees.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The explicit noun prevents reference back to trees.

lessons.title: Forward reference and later identification
lessons.meta: Using a pronoun before its identifying expression
examples: Before he spoke, Mr Li checked his notes.
When she entered, the new principal smiled.
The new policy was announced today. It starts next month.

analyses.label: Subject; refers to the new policy

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: he appears first and Mr Li immediately supplies the identity; this is forward reference resolved later.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The identity of she follows immediately in the same sentence, so the reader waits only briefly.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The new policy is established before It continues it, reducing tracking effort in exposition.

rules: Pronouns usually refer backward, but some styles allow them to refer forward to a later noun phrase.
A forward reference must be resolved quickly by a clear identifying expression, or readers lose orientation.
Formal exposition normally introduces the noun first and then uses a pronoun, avoiding unnecessary forward-reference load.

questions.question: Who does he refer forward to?
questions.correct: The following main-clause subject identifies the referent.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The following main-clause subject identifies the referent.

questions.question: Why is this forward reference understandable?

options.text: The identity appears only in the next paragraph

questions.correct: The identifying phrase is immediate and clear.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The identifying phrase is immediate and clear.

questions.question: Which order better suits exposition?
questions.correct: The entity is established before pronoun continuation.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The entity is established before pronoun continuation.

lessons.title: Reference distance and multiple candidates
lessons.meta: Greater distance and more candidates require fuller naming
examples: The survey began in May. Several teams collected data through summer. After three revisions, the survey was published.
The doctor spoke to the patient after the nurse arrived. She then explained the result.
The doctor spoke to the patient. The nurse then explained the result.

analyses.text: The survey began in May. Several teams collected data through summer.
analyses.label: Prior context
Subject; repeats a distant topic noun

analyses.text: The doctor spoke to the patient after the nurse arrived.
analyses.label: Clause/sentence information

analyses.text: The doctor spoke to the patient.
analyses.label: Clause/sentence information

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: After several intervening nouns, repeating the survey reactivates the distant topic.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: She may denote doctor or nurse; nearest-noun guessing cannot replace semantic and discourse reasoning.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The revision names The nurse, leaving only one performer for the second action.

rules: When a pronoun is far from its antecedent, working-memory load increases; repeat a name or noun phrase.
The nearest noun is not an absolute rule; combine agreement, semantic role and discourse topic.
With multiple candidates, reorder, repeat role names or split sentences so each pronoun has one plausible antecedent.

questions.wrong: Check the rule: Repeating the noun reactivates the topic.

options.text: Yes; it must mean nearest nurse
No; doctor and nurse may both fit

questions.correct: Context or a repeated role noun is needed.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Context or a repeated role noun is needed.

questions.correct: It explicitly assigns the second action to the nurse.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: It explicitly assigns the second action to the nurse.

lessons.title: Integrated cohesion revision
lessons.meta: Check reference, lexis, logic, information status and topic chains sentence by sentence
examples: Lily emailed Anna after she arrived. Anna arrived first, so Lily emailed her.
The method is cheap. However, it is unreliable.
A new bus route opened last month. The service has shortened many commutes.

analyses.text: Lily emailed Anna after she arrived.
analyses.label: Clause/sentence information
Subject; performer in the later clause

analyses.text: A new bus route opened last month.
analyses.label: Paragraph topic
Subject; summary reference to bus route

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The original she has two candidates; the revision adds event order and names, making her uniquely refer to Anna.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: cheap is normally positive and unreliable qualifies it, so However accurately marks contrast.

exampleNotes.title: Discourse focus
exampleNotes.body: The service summarizes bus route and attaches shortened commutes as new information.

rules: In integrated revision, first mark every pronoun and demonstrative and assign one unique antecedent to each.
Next inspect each inter-sentence relation; the connector must accurately mark addition, contrast, result, example or summary.
Finally check that the paragraph adds new information around a stable topic, removing pronouns without antecedents, conceptual drift and repeated conclusions.

questions.question: What does the revision mainly fix?
questions.correct: Names and event order make her refer uniquely to Anna.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Names and event order make her refer uniquely to Anna.

options.text: Yes; the second sentence qualifies the first benefit
No; an example marker is required

questions.correct: cheap and unreliable form an evaluative contrast.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: cheap and unreliable form an evaluative contrast.

questions.question: What cohesive role does The service have?

options.text: It switches to an unrelated topic
It summarizes the referent and introduces a new effect

questions.correct: service continues bus route while adding commute information.
